title: Amazon Kindle

wiki_excerpt:
Amazon Kindle is a series of e-readers designed and marketed by Amazon. Amazon Kindle devices enable users to browse, buy, download, and read e-books, newspapers, magazines,  Audible audiobooks, and other digital media via wireless networking to the Kindle Store. The hardware platform, which Amazon subsidiary Lab126 developed, began as a single device in 2007. Currently, it comprises a range of devices, including e-readers with E Ink electronic paper displays and Kindle applications on all major computing platforms. All Kindle devices integrate with Windows and macOS file systems and Kindle Store content and, as of March 2018, the store had over six million e-books available in the United States.


Naming and development
In 2004, Amazon founder and CEO Jeff Bezos instructed the company's employees to build the world's best electronic reader before Amazon's competitors could. Amazon originally used the codename Fiona for the device.
Branding consultants Michael Cronan and Karin Hibma devised the Kindle name. Lab126 asked them to name the product, and they suggested "kindle", meaning to light a fire. They felt this was an apt metaphor for reading and intellectual excitement.
Kindle hardware evolved from the original Kindle introduced in 2007 and the Kindle DX (with its larger 9.7" screen) introduced in 2009. The DX remained the only non-6" E Ink Kindle device until the 2017 introduction of the Oasis 2. The range included early generation devices with a keyboard (Kindle Keyboard), devices with touch-sensitive, lighted, high-resolution screens (Kindle Paperwhite), early generations of a tablet computer with the Kindle app (Kindle Fire), and low-priced devices with a touch-sensitive screen (Kindle 7). However, the Kindle e-reader has often been a narrow-purpose device for reading rather than being multipurpose hardware that might create distractions while reading. Active Content support was introduced in 2010 only to be dropped from new Kindle devices in late 2014. After the first three generations, the Kindle Fire tablet branding was changed to Amazon Fire in 2014; this name change reflected their wider capabilities as an Android-derived tablet. Other later developments include devices with larger E Ink displays such as the Kindle Oasis 2 (2017) at 7" and the Paperwhite 5 (2021) at 6.8", as well as a device with a 10.2" screen and Wacom stylus support called the Kindle Scribe (2022). In 2022 Amazon also introduced the 11th gen Kindle with a 300 PPI display, ending the use of the 6" 167 PPI display that had been on every basic Kindle since 2007. In 2024 Amazon introduced the first color E Ink Kindle, the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition. In 2025 Amazon updated the Scribe lineup with a new design and introduced a Scribe Colorsoft model.
Amazon has also released Kindle apps for a wide range of devices and platforms, including Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, BlackBerry 10 and Windows Phone. Amazon also has a cloud reader to allow users to read e-books us
grok_lead: The Amazon Kindle is a series of portable e-book readers and associated software ecosystem developed and marketed by Amazon, first released on November 19, 2007, with a high-resolution electronic paper (E Ink) display simulating the appearance of ink on paper and wireless connectivity for downloading content directly to the device. The initial model sold out within 5.5 hours of launch, offering access to 90,000 titles at debut and pioneering features like built-in text-to-speech and expansive storage for up to 1,500 books in subsequent iterations. Subsequent generations introduced innovations such as front-lit displays for low-light reading, waterproofing, and higher pixel densities up to 300 ppi, alongside extended battery life lasting weeks on a single charge, making Kindle devices lightweight and eye-friendly alternatives to traditional paper books. The platform's integration with the Kindle Store has facilitated seamless purchasing and reading of e-books, newspapers, and magazines, while services like Kindle Direct Publishing (launched in 2007) have democratized self-publishing, allowing authors to reach global audiences without traditional gatekeepers. Whispersync for Voice enables synchronization between e-book reading and audiobook listening, enhancing accessibility via Amazon's Audible integration. Kindle has profoundly impacted the publishing industry by accelerating the shift to digital formats, with Amazon capturing approximately 68% of the global e-book market share (rising to 83% including Kindle Unlimited subscriptions), driven by instant access, vast libraries exceeding millions of titles, and subscription models offering unlimited reading for a monthly fee. Notable achievements include enabling multilingual support in over 30 languages and fostering innovations like Kindle Unlimited, launched in 2014 with initial access to over 600,000 titles, which has expanded reading options amid growing e-book revenues projected to reach $14.9 billion globally in 2025. However, the platform has faced controversies, including disputes with publishers over pricing that led to antitrust scrutiny and shifts to agency models, as well as user concerns over digital ownership following recent policy changes in 2025 that discontinued USB file transfers for Kindle books, restricting access to app-based or device-specific downloads and prompting backlash regarding true control of purchased content. These issues highlight tensions between convenience and user autonomy in Amazon's closed ecosystem, though empirical adoption data underscores Kindle's enduring dominance in transforming reading habits through empirical advantages in portability and selection.
